name: Cerne Abbas Giant

attributes.attribute: a turf-cut figure of a man more than 200 feet tall
bears no name and has no known creator
linked to fertility because of its 30-foot erection
carries a huge club held aloft

sources: Newman, Paul. Gods and Graven Images: The Chalk Hill-Figures of Britain. London: Robert Hale, 1987, 72–101.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Cerne Abbas Giant is a British mythological site and folkloric figure. It stands on a hill near the village of Cerne Abbas in Dorset, England. Workers removed the green turf down to the chalky white soil. The figure outlines a man more than 200 feet tall. It bears no name. No one knows who carved it. The White Horse of Uffington is another turf-cut figure. Scholars have dated that figure to the Iron Age. They do not know whether the Cerne Abbas Giant comes from the same period. Most scholars think the Giant was already cut into the hillside when the Celtic tribe the Durotriges arrived. Some argue his features tie him to other Celtic mythologies. His erection is 30 feet long. This led to an assumed connection with fertility. A local belief held that the Giant helped women become pregnant. Outdoor meetings on or near the figure were common for this reason. The Giant carries a huge club held aloft. The Irish god Dagda carried a similar club. The continental Celtic god Sucellus also carried a mallet-like weapon.

okr.objective: The Cerne Abbas Giant is a nameless turf-cut figure of a man on a Dorset hill.
key_results: It is more than 200 feet tall, cut in white chalk near the village of Cerne Abbas.
No one knows its name or who carved it.
Its 30-foot erection links it to local fertility beliefs.
It carries a club like the Irish god Dagda and the god Sucellus.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
